title.narrative: Provision of Mobile Health Clinic to Municipality of Beirut

description.narrative: While all cities suffered during 2020, Beirut experienced one of its worst years on record. Already coping with an unprecedented displacement crisis, the city added an economic crisis and the Covid-19 public health crisis on top of it. An estimated one in four people in Lebanon is a refugee, with thousands of refugees, stateless people, and vulnerable domestic workers residing in Beirut itself. Already strained by the demand on public services, the Government of Lebanon defaulted on its foreign debt, resulting in a drastic decrease in the value of the Lebanese Lira and a drastic increase in poverty levels throughout the country. These economic conditions worsened further with the onset of Covid-19, which pushed one of every three Lebanese households into unemployment, according to a World Health Organization survey. These crises came to a head on August 4th, 2020, when the explosion in Beirut’s port killed 200 people, injured more than 6,500 and damaged over 74,000 homes, affecting more than 290,000 people, including many refugees and migrant domestic workers. Since then, Beirut’s residents have struggled to receive the medical attention they need both in the aftermath of the blast and as the city continues to cope with the prevalence of Covid-19. With so many vulnerable Beirutis unable to access healthcare due to limited financial resources or the means to access private or public health facilities, the Municipality of Beirut is bringing healthcare to them. The Municipality will use the Global Cities Fund to purchase and operate its first Municipal Mobile Health Clinic, which will provide free and non-discriminatory Covid-19 testing to individuals who are unable to access basic medical services due to lack of transportation, lack of finances, or other barriers to care. When the opportunity arises within Lebanon, the Municipal Mobile Health Clinic will also provide Covid-19 inoculation services. The clinic will go where it is needed most, focusing on neighborhoods with high populations of refugees, migrants, and vulnerable Lebanese that were severely impacted by the August 4th explosion, such as those working-class neighborhoods bordering the port. The project will also raise awareness on good Covid-19 prevention measures within vulnerable neighborhoods through the production and dissemination of WhatsApp messaging, video campaigns, close coordination with local civil society and non-government agencies, and other targeted awareness raising strategies. While over $500M in foreign aid has poured into Lebanon following the August 4th explosion, the vast majority has gone to international or national actors, with a fraction left for the Municipality of Beirut and civil society organizations operating within the city. Through this project, the Municipality will directly channel international funding to the most vulnerable Beirutis, regardless of immigration status.
